commenti.body:
1. The Last Emperor
2. Amadeus
3. Platoon
4. Gandhi
5. Out of Africa
6. Ordinary People
7. Terms of Endearment
8. Rain Man
9. Chariots of Fire
10. Driving Miss Daisy

I think there's quite a spread in quality across these ten titles. The Last Emperor and Amadeus are masterpieces. The middle titles vary from excellent to solid. The bottom film is pretty bad.

Out of Africa is the 1980s Best Picture winners what The English Patient was the 1990s ones. Those are both exceptionally well-made films with a lot of heart, but they're just too serious and sentimental for a lot of people. If it isn't their cup of tea, fine, but if they want to argue that they are badly-made films, they are wrong.

Amadeus is one of the most rewatchable and entertaining movies I've ever seen. It grabs you immediately and you can't look away for three hours.

I saw Platoon after a lot of other Vietnam movies so I don't think it struck me as much as it did other people, but it's a very good movie and I respect its importance in the canon.

I think Ordinary People is actually quite terrific, but I do wish Raging Bull had won. That would have been in the first or second position on the list, imho.

False premise as far as "Amadeus" goes. Wildly entertaining, iconic (especially among music types).  Culturally significant. Amadeus hasn't lost an ounce of luster since its release.

I'd argue the same for Chariots. 

"Rain Man" may have been a product of its time. It's 80s esthetic dates it, and it's big selling point at the time was "Dustin Hoffman plays an autistic savant!".

I'd agree on "Ordinary People". At the time, the big deal was "Mary Tyler Moore plays against type." Nowadays, "ordinary people" don't even remember MTM or what her type was.

Platoon was a good movie about Vietnam, but all 'Nam movies have to live in the shadow of "Apocalypse Now"

I haven't seen 2,5,6,7, and 9. As far as I can tell, there are some glaring omissions like Scorsese never winning best picture, but there's nothing terrible like when Crash beat Brokeback Mountain. None of them would have been my first choice, but Amadeus and Gandhi are among my favorites. 

If I chose the winners: Raging Bull, Son of the White Mare, The King of Comedy, L'argent, Paris Texas, A Time to Live a Time to Die, Blue Velvet, The Emperor's Naked Army Marches On, The Decalogue or A Short Film About Killing, The Seventh Continent

Woof.  There are some real dogs there.  Amadeus is really the only one of those I return to.

As far as them losing their luster, I think that says less about the decade and more about the picker.  The Academy has always been quick to congratulate themselves on a film with some bland take on an important issue, or a dry history lesson, or a yearning doomed romance, or all of the above, preferably featuring period costumes and lush scenery, and a character with a disability.

I mean, the list of best picture winners in the 70s isn't fantastic either.  You don't hear a lot about Kramer Vs. Kramer, or The Sting, or Patten these days.  I saw French Connection for the first time shortly after the death of George Floyd, and it was an uncomfortable watch.  Meanwhile this is the decade that gave us Spielberg and George Lucas and Scorsese and Altman, and they are nowhere to be found on that list.  Coppola basically single-handedly saved the day for New Hollywood at the Oscars in the 70s.

So yes, I suspect the Academy will continue to make safe picks that largely ignore the crackling energy of newcomers and outsiders, only occasionally picking something undeniably brilliant, and that those safe picks will inevitably fall by the wayside as time passes.

As to what that looks like, Sight And Sound's latest poll of the best movies ever has 4 American films from the 80s in the top 100:  Do The Right Thing, Blade Runner, Blue Velvet, The Shining.  Raging Bull is in the second 100, along with popcorn movies like Raiders Of The Lost Ark and The Thing.  That's already a much more exciting slate of films than the Academy picked.  And that's not just decades worth of perspective talking — a lot of people, myself included, liked those films more at the time, too.

But I think what made the 80s great, and this is with the perspective that comes with time passing, was that it was the high water mark of practical effects.  Directors had the budget and technology to make fantastic worlds come to life in a way they never had before, before CGI started to take hold.  The Academy was never going to celebrate Back To The Future, or Ghostbusters, or Raiders Of The Lost Ark, The Empire Strikes Back, The Thing, The Princess Bride, The Terminator, Aliens.  But that stuff really is the enduring heart of 80s Hollywood.

Amadeus is a masterpiece. Platoon, Ordinary People, Terms of Endearment, & Rain Man are fantastic. The other films are of varying quality but they all have at least one good element. For example Driving Miss Daisy has wonderful performances.
